papers.title: Multiscale multimodal integration of spatial omics through a deep generative model with CORAL.
papers.summary: This paper presents CORAL, a deep generative model designed to integrate spatial omics data across multiple scales and modalities, such as spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics. The method aims to combine datasets with different resolutions and molecular readouts into a unified representation, allowing researchers to analyze tissue architecture more comprehensively. Although the abstract provided is minimal, the core contribution appears to be a computational framework for multiscale, multimodal spatial data fusion.
papers.why: This tool could help integrate spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics data at different resolutions to study mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, interneurons, and perineuronal nets within complex brain tissue.
papers.figure: Figure showing the CORAL model architecture and its workflow for integrating multiscale, multimodal spatial omics datasets.

papers.title: Chaperone-mediated autophagy targets Miro-1 for degradation to promote mitophagy and inhibit α-synuclein induced ferroptosis
papers.summary: This paper investigates how chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) degrades Miro-1, a protein that anchors mitochondria to the cytoskeleton, as a way to trigger mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria). The study connects this process to α-synuclein, a protein implicated in Parkinson's disease, showing that promoting Miro-1 degradation and mitophagy can block ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death linked to α-synuclein toxicity. Overall, the findings suggest a protective mechanism where CMA-mediated mitophagy counteracts neurodegeneration-associated cell death pathways.
papers.why: This paper provides mechanistic insight into mitophagy regulation in neurons, directly relevant to understanding how autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria protects against neurodegeneration-related cell death.

papers.title: Engineered autophagy receptors for selective protein clearance in neurodegeneration.
papers.summary: This paper discusses the design of engineered autophagy receptors, which are proteins modified to specifically target disease-causing proteins for degradation via autophagy. These synthetic receptors could help clear toxic protein aggregates that accumulate in neurodegenerative diseases. The approach aims to enhance or redirect the cell's natural clearance machinery toward harmful substrates that are normally resistant to removal.
papers.why: Engineered autophagy receptors directly relate to selective autophagy mechanisms in neurons, offering potential tools or conceptual frameworks relevant to studying mitophagy and protein clearance pathways in neuronal subtypes like interneurons.
papers.figure: A schematic showing the design and mechanism of the engineered autophagy receptor binding its target and autophagy machinery.

papers.title: Chronic Post-Stroke Cognitive Impairment: Microglial Autophagy, PI3K/Akt/mTOR Signaling, and Persistent Neuroinflammation.
papers.summary: This paper investigates chronic cognitive impairment following stroke, focusing on how microglia—brain immune cells—use autophagy to manage their response to injury. It examines the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway, a key regulator of autophagy and cell survival, as a driver of ongoing inflammation in the brain after stroke. The work links sustained neuroinflammation and dysregulated microglial autophagy to long-term cognitive decline in stroke survivors.
papers.why: Although focused on microglia rather than neurons, this paper's exploration of autophagy pathway regulation (PI3K/Akt/mTOR) in the brain offers mechanistic insight transferable to neuronal mitophagy/autophagy studies and inflammation-related effects on interneuron and perineuronal net integrity.

papers.title: Refined on-tissue chemical derivatization expands MALDI-MSI capabilities for spatial metabolomics of mammalian organs and metastatic tumors using EDC and 4-APEBA.
papers.summary: This paper describes an improved chemical labeling method applied directly on tissue slices before MALDI mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI), using two reagents called EDC and 4-APEBA. These chemical tags help detect small metabolite molecules that are normally hard to see with this imaging technique, improving sensitivity and coverage. The method was tested on mammalian organs and metastatic tumor samples, showing better spatial mapping of metabolites across tissue sections.
papers.why: This technique could enhance spatial metabolomics workflows applicable to brain tissue, helping map metabolic changes around neurons, interneurons, and perineuronal nets alongside autophagy/mitophagy studies.
papers.figure: A representative MALDI-MSI image comparing metabolite detection before and after EDC/4-APEBA derivatization in tissue sections.

papers.title: Tumor Suppressor RASSF8 Orchestrates Cellular Autophagy Through Activation of the AMPK/ULK1 Axis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the tumor suppressor protein RASSF8 regulates autophagy, the cellular process of degrading and recycling components. The researchers found that RASSF8 activates the AMPK/ULK1 signaling pathway, which is a well-known trigger for initiating autophagy. This suggests RASSF8 plays a role in controlling cellular quality control mechanisms, potentially linking tumor suppression to autophagic regulation.
papers.why: While focused on cancer biology, the AMPK/ULK1 axis is a core autophagy initiation pathway relevant to understanding mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in neurons, even though this study is in a non-neuronal context.

papers.title: Paeoniflorin ameliorates Parkinson's disease by promoting autophagy to inhibit A1 phenotype astrocyte activation.
papers.summary: This study investigates paeoniflorin, a plant-derived compound, as a potential treatment for Parkinson's disease. The researchers found that it works by boosting autophagy, the cell's internal recycling process, which in turn suppresses the formation of harmful 'A1' type astrocytes. Since A1 astrocytes are known to damage neurons, reducing their activation helped protect brain cells in their disease model.
papers.why: While focused on astrocytes rather than neurons, this paper is relevant because it mechanistically links autophagy modulation to neuroprotection in Parkinson's disease, offering a comparative pathway perspective for the project's focus on autophagy/mitophagy in neurons.

papers.title: Integrated multi-omics identifies PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte state remodeling in paraquat-associated Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: This study uses integrated multi-omics approaches to investigate how paraquat exposure, a known environmental risk factor for Parkinson's disease, affects brain cell populations. The researchers identified a specific state of mature oligodendrocytes marked by high PTGDS expression that becomes remodeled or altered in paraquat-associated Parkinson's disease. This finding suggests that oligodendrocytes, not just neurons, may play an important role in the disease process triggered by this pesticide exposure.
papers.why: While focused on oligodendrocytes rather than neurons directly, this paper's multi-omics approach to identifying disease-associated glial cell states in a neurodegenerative model could inform spatial transcriptomics strategies and analytical frameworks relevant to studying neuron-glia interactions in the brain.
